Contentious

kun-TEN-shus -- shares a root with 'contend,' meaning to compete or argue. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Contentious is likely to cause disagreement or argument; controversial.

Whether to raise property taxes remained the most contentious issue at the town meeting.

Worked Example

Every time the topic of realigning district lines comes up at a school board meeting, the room erupts into heated arguments that last well past midnight.

That tendency to spark heated disagreement is exactly what contentious describes. Unlike 'popular,' which nearly everyone agrees on, a contentious issue divides people sharply.

How Contentious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disputed

disputed: argued about or questioned

controversial

controversial: causing public disagreement

divisive

divisive: causing disagreement or hostility between people

Antonyms

uncontroversial

uncontroversial: not likely to cause disagreement

agreeable

agreeable: pleasant and easy to get along with

How Strong Is It? — disputed → contentious → divisive

disputed vs. contentious

disputed vs. contentious: Disputed is milder than contentious -- something disputed is simply questioned or argued over, while contentious implies the disagreement is heated and ongoing.

divisive vs. contentious

divisive vs. contentious: Divisive can feel stronger than contentious: contentious describes an issue likely to spark argument, while divisive suggests it actually splits people into opposing sides.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — con-

prefix — con-: together, with (Latin)

root — -tent-

root — -tent-: to strive, stretch (from Latin tendere; its stem appears as -tent- here and as tens- in tension)

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of; characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin contendere meant 'to strive together' or 'compete,' from con- ('together') and tendere ('to stretch, strive') -- spelled -tent- here -- plus -ious ('full of'). Something contentious, at its root, invites people to strive against one another -- the same root that gives us tension.

Use the root in a new word: tension

Use the root in a new word: tension: You could feel the tension in the room the moment the two rival candidates walked in together.

Word Choice

Contentious is common in political, legal, and academic writing to describe issues, debates, or relationships marked by ongoing disagreement.
